back:
Headline: array is fixed-size storage with no heap allocation; vector is one contiguous heap block that grows at the back; deque is a sequence of fixed-size blocks, O(1) at both ends, random access but not contiguous; list is a doubly linked list, one heap node per element, O(1) insert and erase at a known position, no random access.
Output:
24 4 0 0
3 2
The sizeof(a) is 3 doubles = 24 bytes. d is {0,1,2,3} after push_front, so d[2] is 2.
Interview trap: a Python list is a dynamic array, so people assume std::list is the analogue. In C++ it is the rarely-fast choice: every element is a separate heap node, and iteration chases pointers. Default to vector.

front: Big-O of the core containers. {{c1::push_back on a std::vector is amortised O(1)}}; lookup in a {{c2::std::map is O(log n)}}; lookup in a {{c3::std::unordered_map is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case}}.
back:
ContainerIndex / accessInsert or eraseFindNotes
vectorO(1)O(1) amortised at back; O(n) in middleO(n) unsortedcontiguous
dequeO(1)O(1) at both ends; O(n) middleO(n)blocked storage
listnoneO(1) given an iteratorO(n)node per element
arrayO(1)n/a (fixed size)O(n)stack storage
map / setnoneO(log n)O(log n)red-black tree, ordered
unordered_map / setnoneO(1) averageO(1) average, O(n) worsthash table
priority_queuetop O(1)push and pop O(log n)n/abinary heap over a vector

Headline: they are container adaptors: a restricted interface over an underlying sequence. stack and queue wrap a deque by default. priority_queue wraps a vector as a binary heap; the default comparator std::less gives a max-heap, and std::greater gives a min-heap.
Output:
stack top 3
stack top 2
max: 5 4 2 1
min: 1 2 4 5
The adaptors expose no iterators and no operator[].
Interview trap: you cannot remove or re-prioritise an arbitrary element in a priority_queue. Dijkstra-style code pushes a fresh entry and skips stale ones on pop (lazy deletion).

front: Both a std::vector<double> and a std::list<double> of length 10 million are O(n) to sum. Why is the vector loop usually several times faster?
back:
Headline: Big-O hides the constant, and the constant is set by memory layout. A vector is one contiguous block, so consecutive elements share cache lines (64 bytes on x86, so 8 doubles per line), and the hardware prefetcher streams them. A list element is a separate heap node that holds two pointers (16 bytes of overhead) plus the value, and each step is a dependent load that often misses cache.
Contiguity also lets the compiler vectorise the loop with SIMD.
Interview trap: 'why vector, not list?' is answered by cache behaviour, not by complexity. Insertion in the middle of a vector is O(n) and still often wins for n up to a few thousand, because memmove is fast.

Headline: capacity doubles when it is exhausted (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 here). reserve(n) changes capacity, not size, and it does not change size().
Output:
initial capacity 0
size 1 -> capacity 1
size 2 -> capacity 2
size 3 -> capacity 4
size 5 -> capacity 8
size 9 -> capacity 16
size 17 -> capacity 32
reserve(20): capacity 20, size 0
after 20 push_back: capacity 20
The growth factor is an implementation choice (libstdc++ and libc++ use 2; MSVC uses 1.5), so the exact sequence is not part of the standard.
Interview trap: r.reserve(20); r[0] = 1; compiles and is undefined behaviour, because no element exists. Reserve is a capacity hint, not a resize. Use resize or push_back.

front: Derive why push_back is amortised O(1) on a std::vector that doubles its capacity when full. Give the total number of element moves for n pushes.
back:
Derivation. A reallocation happens when the size reaches a power of two, at sizes \(1,2,4,\dots,2^k\) with \(2^k\le n\). Each such reallocation copies (or moves) every element that exists at that time:
\[\text{moves}\le \sum_{j=0}^{k}2^j = 2^{k+1}-1 \le 2n.\]Add the \(n\) placements and the total is below \(3n\), so the amortised cost per push_back is at most 3 moves: \(O(1)\).
For a general growth factor \(g>1\), the copy total is about \(n\,g/(g-1)\): \(g=2\) gives \(2n\), \(g=1.5\) gives \(3n\). Any constant \(g>1\) is amortised O(1).
Where it breaks: if the element type's move constructor is not noexcept, vector copies on reallocation (it uses move_if_noexcept to keep the strong exception guarantee), which can turn each reallocation into an expensive copy.
Interviewer follow-up: why does the standard not fix the growth factor? Because it only requires amortised constant time, which any constant factor above 1 gives.

front: std::map and std::set are implemented as a {{c1::red-black tree}}, so lookup, insert and erase are {{c2::O(log n) worst case}}, and iteration visits keys in {{c3::sorted order}}.
back:
The tree gives a worst-case height bound of about \(2\log_2(n+1)\), which is why the worst case is O(log n) with no hashing. Keys need a strict weak ordering (operator< or a comparator), not equality alone. You get lower_bound, upper_bound and range scans for free.
Cost: one heap node per element with three pointers and a colour, so memory and cache behaviour are worse than a vector. An order book depth ladder is the natural use: the first element is the best price.

front: For std::unordered_map the load factor is {{c1::size divided by bucket_count}}, the default max_load_factor is {{c2::1.0}}, and an insert that would exceed it triggers a {{c3::rehash into a larger bucket array, which costs O(n)}}.

back:
Headline: input, output, forward, bidirectional, random access (C++20 adds contiguous). Random access means it + n, it[i] and it1 - it2 in O(1). std::sort needs random access, so it works on vector, deque and array, not on list. list is bidirectional and provides its own member sort().
Output:
1
1
1 2 3 
1 2 3
The first two lines are the is_same_v checks against the iterator tags.
Interview trap: with C++20 ranges, std::ranges::sort needs a random-access range too. A std::sort on a list does not compile, and the error message is long: look for the iterator concept, not the template.

front: Iterator invalidation: a {{c1::std::vector push_back that reallocates}} invalidates all iterators, pointers and references; erase on a vector invalidates iterators {{c2::at and after the erased position}}; an unordered_map {{c3::rehash invalidates iterators but not references to elements}}.
back:
OperationInvalidates
vector push_back (reallocates)all iterators, pointers, references
vector push_back (no reallocation)only end()
vector insert / eraseat and after the point of change
list insertnothing
list eraseonly the erased element
map / set insertnothing
map / set eraseonly the erased element
unordered_map insert (rehash)all iterators; references and pointers survive
unordered_map eraseonly the erased element
Rule of thumb: an iterator held across a modifying call is dead unless the table says otherwise.

Headline: v.erase(it) invalidates it, and the element that moves into its slot is then skipped by ++it. The loop also keeps going after the end is reached, so the program has undefined behaviour.
Run as written (g++ 13, -O2), it segfaults (exit code 139). Built with -fsanitize=address, AddressSanitizer reports heap-buffer-overflow with a READ of size 4 at line 7, the *it dereference.
The expected output would be 1 3 5; the code gives no such guarantee.
Interview trap: 'it works on my small test' proves nothing about undefined behaviour. Fix it with the erase-return idiom, the erase-remove idiom or std::erase_if (next card).

Headline: three correct forms. (A) it = v.erase(it), which returns the next valid iterator, with the increment only in the else branch. (B) the erase-remove idiom, v.erase(std::remove_if(...), v.end()), which predates C++20. (C) std::erase_if(container, pred) (C++20), which works on vector, deque, list, map, unordered_map, set and string, and returns the number of elements removed.
Output:
1 3 5 
1 3 5 
1 3 5 
1a 3c 
unordered removed 2, left 2
For a map, erase(it) returns the iterator after the erased element, since C++11, so the same pattern applies.
Interview trap: m.erase(it++) is the correct C++03 idiom for a map. The same expression on a vector skips an element, because the erase shifts the next one into the slot just vacated. v.erase(std::unique(...)) with one argument compiles and erases only one element; the two-argument form is needed.

front: std::stable_sort is a {{c1::merge sort}} that keeps equal elements in their input order. std::sort is an {{c2::introsort}} and is {{c3::not stable}}.
back:
Complexity: sort is O(N log N) comparisons. stable_sort is N log N with enough extra memory, and N log² N without it. libstdc++'s introsort is quicksort, switches to heapsort when the recursion depth exceeds about 2 log₂ n, and uses insertion sort for short runs. Output of the snippet:
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Trade { int id; int desk; };

int main() {
    std::vector<Trade> trades;
    for (int i = 0; i < 40; ++i) trades.push_back({100 + i, (i * 7) % 3});  // desks 0,1,2
    auto byDesk = [](const Trade& a, const Trade& b) { return a.desk < b.desk; };

    auto s1 = trades;
    std::sort(s1.begin(), s1.end(), byDesk);            // introsort: not stable
    auto s2 = trades;
    std::stable_sort(s2.begin(), s2.end(), byDesk);     // merge sort: ties keep input order

    std::cout << "stable_sort, desk 0 ids:";
    for (const auto& t : s2) if (t.desk == 0) std::cout << ' ' << t.id;
    std::cout << "\nsort,        desk 0 ids:";
    for (const auto& t : s1) if (t.desk == 0) std::cout << ' ' << t.id;
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:
stable_sort, desk 0 ids: 100 103 106 109 112 115 118 121 124 127 130 133 136 139
sort,        desk 0 ids: 100 121 118 124 115 127 112 130 109 133 106 136 103 139
For a multi-key sort, sort by the secondary key first and then stable_sort by the primary key, or write a comparator with an explicit tie-break.
Interview trap: in this libstdc++ build sort is insertion sort up to 16 elements and keeps the order there, so a small test looks stable. At 17 or more elements it does not. Test with realistic sizes.

Headline: std::nth_element(first, first+k, last) places the k-th smallest element at position k, with everything before it no larger and everything after it no smaller. Average cost is linear, against n log n for a full sort; at n = 10,000 that is roughly 13 times fewer comparisons, ignoring constants.
Here the 1% quantile is the 101st smallest (index 100). VaR is the negative of that P&L, and ES is the average of the worst 1% outcomes, which are the 100 values below index 100.
Output:
1% quantile P&L = -4899.0 k
99% VaR = 4899.0 k
99% ES  = 4949.5 k
Check: the worst 100 values are \(-4999,\dots,-4900\), whose mean is \(-4949.5\).
Interviewer follow-up: why does the quantile convention matter? Index \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) and interpolated quantiles differ by one or more scenarios at 99% with small samples.
Interview trap: after nth_element the two sides are only partitioned, not sorted, so do not read "the 2nd worst" from them. For several quantiles from one sample, sort once or call nth_element on the shrinking subrange.

front: std::partial_sort(first, middle, last) leaves the {{c1::smallest (middle - first) elements}} sorted at the front, at cost {{c2::O(N log M)}} where M is the size of the front block.
back: Compared with the alternatives for a top-10 of a million values: partial_sort is about N log 10; nth_element then sort on the front 10 is O(N) plus 10 log 10; a full sort is N log N. The elements behind middle are in unspecified order. Use partial_sort when the front block must be ordered and the rest does not matter.

Headline: lower_bound returns the first element not less than x (index 1 for x = 0.5). upper_bound returns the first element greater than x (index 2). They differ only when x equals a pillar. For interpolation, the segment is upper_bound - 1, so x = 0.5 uses the pillars 0.5 and 1, with the helper clamping at both ends.
Output:
x=0.1  lower_bound=0  upper_bound=0  bracket=0
x=0.5  lower_bound=1  upper_bound=2  bracket=1
x=1.5  lower_bound=3  upper_bound=3  bracket=2
x=10  lower_bound=5  upper_bound=6  bracket=4
x=12  lower_bound=6  upper_bound=6  bracket=4
Both run in O(log n) on a sorted vector. For x beyond the last pillar, the helper clamps to the last segment, which is extrapolation and must be a deliberate choice.
Interview trap: lower_bound(x) - 1 is the common off-by-one. For x exactly on a pillar it picks the segment to the left, which changes the interpolated value at every pillar.

Headline: accumulate is a strict left fold, so it computes \(((0+10^{16})+1)-10^{16}\). Near \(10^{16}\) the double spacing is 2, so \(10^{16}+1\) rounds back to \(10^{16}\) and the sum is 0. reduce may group the operations in any order because it requires an associative and commutative operation. The regrouping \((10^{16}-10^{16})+1\) gives 1.
Output:
accumulate: 0
regrouped:  1
reduce:     0
In this libstdc++ build reduce happened to run left to right and printed 0; the standard permits 1.
Interview trap: std::reduce with std::execution::par_unseq can change its result with thread count, so a risk number can differ between runs. For reproducible aggregation use accumulate, a fixed-tree pairwise sum, or Kahan compensation.

Headline: inner_product is a fold of pairwise products: \(\sum_i a_i b_i\) plus init. Here a is GBP P&L per +1bp in each bucket and b is the parallel shift in bp, so the result is the scenario P&L: \((-1200)(5)+(-800)(-3)+(300)(2)=-3000\).
transform applies a unary function and writes into an output range, so the shifts are converted to decimal rates (5bp becomes 0.0005).
Output:
P&L = -3000.0 GBP
0.0005 -0.0003 0.0002
Both are single-pass, O(n), and read the inputs once.
Interview trap: the type of init is the accumulator type. Passing 0 instead of 0.0 makes the sum an int, so every partial result is truncated. Always pass a double.

Headline: std::unique removes only consecutive duplicates, so it needs sorted input for a full dedupe. The first output line shows 3 1 2 3 1, which keeps the non-adjacent 3 and 1 that reappear. std::partition reorders so that elements satisfying the predicate come first, returns an iterator to the start of the second block, and is not stable.
Output:
3 1 2 3 1 
evens: 3
first block all even: true
The count of evens is deterministic. The order inside each block is not part of the contract, so do not print it. Use std::stable_partition when order matters.
Interview trap: v.erase(std::unique(v.begin(), v.end())); compiles and erases one element, not the duplicates. Use the two-argument erase.

Headline: a by-value capture copies the variable when the lambda is created, and the copy is const inside the lambda unless it is mutable. A by-reference capture holds an alias, so the lambda sees later changes. The output is by value: 10 and by ref: 25.
A reference capture is only safe while the variable outlives the lambda.
Interview trap: [=] copies every name the body uses, but a this member copies the pointer, not the object. Since C++20, implicit capture of this through [=] is deprecated.

Headline: a by-value capture is a const member of the closure unless the lambda is mutable. A mutable closure changes its own copy, and that state persists across calls to the same closure object. The outer variable is untouched. The output is 1 2 3 then outer calls = 0.
Interview trap: copying a stateful lambda forks its state. A std::function that holds a copy and a second copy of it have independent counters.

Headline: [&start] captures a local by reference. The returned std::function outlives the frame, so the call reads a dead stack slot. This is undefined behaviour.
The plain binary happened to print 1 (correct would be 11). GCC warns about the uninitialised read at -Wall. Under AddressSanitizer with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1 it reports stack-use-after-return at line 6, the ++start.
Fix: capture by value, [start]() mutable { return ++start; }.
Interview trap: the same bug appears with lambdas handed to std::thread, to async callbacks, or stored in a container of event handlers. Capture by value or own the state with std::shared_ptr.

Headline: [this] stores the object's address, so the lambda reads the current value. [*this] (C++17) copies the whole object when the lambda is created, so it keeps the old value. The output is live: 250 and snapshot: 100.
Interview trap: [this] dangles if the object is destroyed or moved while the lambda is alive. It is the same lifetime rule as reference capture, and an asynchronous callback is the usual place it fails. [*this] copies, so it is wrong for types that cannot be copied cheaply.

Headline: a template parameter is inlined with no indirection, but each lambda type generates its own copy of the code. A function pointer costs one indirect call, and only a captureless lambda converts to one. std::function is type-erased: every call is indirect, and a closure larger than the implementation's small buffer (16 bytes in libstdc++) is heap-allocated.
Output:
9 9 6
sizeof(std::function<double(double)>) = 32
sizeof(scaled) = 8
The std::function object itself is 32 bytes in libstdc++.
Interview trap: std::function in an innermost loop blocks inlining and vectorisation. Template the hot path, and use std::function only at configuration boundaries.

front:
std::sort is called on 40 values in {0,1,2} with the comparator [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; }. What happens, and why?
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::mt19937 g(7);
    std::vector<int> v(40);
    for (auto& x : v) x = g() % 3;                                              // 0..2, many duplicates
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; });        // not a strict weak ordering
    std::cout << "sorted " << v.size() << " elements\n";
}
back:
Headline: a comparator must be a strict weak ordering: irreflexive (comp(a,a) is false), transitive, and with transitive incomparability. <= breaks irreflexivity, and libstdc++'s partition loop relies on a sentinel that this comparator can run past. The result is undefined behaviour.
Observed: at -O2 the program segfaults (exit code 139), with no output. With -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG libstdc++ stops with Error: comparison doesn't meet irreflexive requirements, assert(!(a < a)).
Interview trap: the bug needs duplicates and enough elements to reach the partition loop. A test on distinct values passes, which is why it reaches production. Use <, or a key with an explicit tie-break.

Headline: the hash must agree with operator==: equal keys must produce equal hashes. Hash every field that == compares, and no others. The combine step here is the boost-style mix. Output: 2 1260.5, i.e. two keys and the updated value.
Interview trap: a hash that ignores the date sends every trade of one id into one bucket. Lookups then become O(n) and the bug is invisible in correctness tests. Also, never put a mutable field in a key that lives in a hash map.

Headline: the book needs ordered depth, a best price, and fast updates at arbitrary levels. A std::map with std::greater keeps bids in descending price order, so the best bid is begin() in O(1), and an update is O(log n). An unordered_map is O(1) for level lookup but gives no order, so the best price needs a scan or a separate heap. Production books often combine both: a hash for price to level, plus a cached best level.
Output:
best bid 10050 x 300
best ask 10052 x 200
spread 2 ticks
10050:300 10049:200
Keys are integer ticks, so equal prices always compare and hash equal.
Interview trap: bids[price] inserts a default entry if the level is missing, which creates phantom zero-size levels. Query with find, and erase levels that drop to zero.

Headline: an optional carries an explicit 'no value' state, so the type system makes callers handle it. value_or(d) returns the fallback. value() throws std::bad_optional_access. operator* on an empty optional is undefined behaviour and does not throw.
Output:
2.31 -1
false
caught: bad optional access
Interviewer follow-up: what is the cost? Typically one extra flag byte plus alignment padding, with no heap allocation.
Interview trap: a legitimate 0.0 is a value, not 'empty', so do not test if (q) when the stored type can be zero. Test has_value().

Headline: std::visit calls a function object chosen by the active alternative. The usual form is an overload set built from lambdas. The compiler checks exhaustiveness, so a missing alternative fails at compile time. std::get<T> on the wrong alternative throws std::bad_variant_access.
Output:
bond clean 98.5
swap par 3.25%
cds 120bp
3.25
bad access: std::get: wrong index for variant
The variant stores its alternatives inline, with no heap allocation and no vtable. Its size is the largest alternative plus the index.
Interview trap: the variant's size is its largest alternative plus the index, so one large alternative makes every element of a vector<variant> that large. Box the large alternatives, for example with unique_ptr.

Headline: auto [a, b, c] = f(); binds names to the members of the returned tuple, struct or array. auto copies, auto& references, and const auto& references read-only. A loop with auto [k, v] copies each pair, so only the auto& loop changes the map.
Output:
99.25 4.1 3
10y=3.85 2y=3.1 
3.6
The output 3.6 is 3.10 + 0.5, since the first loop's +1.0 went to a copy.
Interview trap: in C++17 a structured binding cannot be captured by a lambda; C++20 allows it. Binding a type with the wrong number of members, or with private ones, is a compile error.

Headline: std::views::filter | std::views::transform | std::views::take composes into one lazy range. Nothing is computed until the loop asks for the next element, and each element flows through filter then transform one at a time. No intermediate vector is allocated, and take stops the pipeline after three hits.
Output:
180 113.25 450
A view does not own its data. It is a cheap object with begin and end, not a container.
Interview trap: views are not cached. Iterating a view twice repeats the work (see the next card). A view over a temporary container dangles (see the card after next).

Headline: the first pass calls the predicate once per element (6 calls). The second pass calls it 4 more times for elements 3 to 6. filter_view caches only begin(), the first match, so the search for the first match is not repeated, but the rest of the sequence is recomputed on each traversal.
Output:
pass 1: sum 12, predicate calls 6
pass 2: sum 24, predicate calls 10
Each traversal re-runs everything that has side effects or is expensive. A std::vector copy (or std::ranges::to in C++23) evaluates it once.
Interview trap: a counter inside a predicate or a transform reports the number of traversals, not the number of elements. Materialise the result if the function is expensive and the range is used more than once.

Headline: std::ranges::dangling, a placeholder type with no dereference operator. A vector rvalue is not a borrowed_range: the iterator would point into a container that is destroyed at the end of the full expression, so the standard returns a placeholder instead of an iterator. Writing *it does not compile.
Output:
result type is std::ranges::dangling: no iterator to dereference
2
The lvalue v is a borrowed range, so find returns a real iterator.
Interview trap: the non-ranges std::find(make().begin(), make().end(), 2) compiles, but its two iterators come from two different temporary vectors, and both are dangling. That is silent undefined behaviour, which the ranges version is designed to prevent.

Headline: duration_cast truncates toward zero, so 1500ms becomes 1 second and -1500ms becomes -1. Mixed units are converted to the common type, here minutes, so 2h + 30min counts 150. A sys_days is a time point counting days since the epoch, so subtracting two of them gives a day count. 2026-03-20 is 78 days after 1 January 2026 and is a Friday.
Output:
1
-1
150
78 days after 1 Jan 2026
Fri
Interviewer follow-up: how do you floor a negative duration to whole seconds? Use floor<seconds>, which rounds down, instead of duration_cast.
Interview trap: duration_cast is truncation, not floor. For a date rule, always use calendar types (year_month_day) rather than counting 30-day months.

Headline: adding months to a year_month_day keeps the day number. 31 February and 31 April do not exist, so the naive results are invalid and ok() returns false. The end-of-month convention uses year_month_day_last, which gives the last day of the target month.
Output:
naive 1: 2026-02-31 is not a valid date invalid
naive 2: 2026-03-31 ok
naive 3: 2026-04-31 is not a valid date invalid
eom 1: 2026-02-28
eom 2: 2026-03-31
eom 3: 2026-04-30
A production schedule also needs business-day adjustment (for example modified following), a holiday calendar, and an explicit rule for whether the end-of-month property is kept.
Interview trap: generating each date from the previous one loses the end-of-month property. Chaining 31 Jan, 28 Feb, then 28 Mar gives the wrong later dates. Always build the k-th date from the anchor date and k months.

Headline: rand() keeps one hidden global state shared by all callers, has a guaranteed maximum of only 32767, and its low bits are weak on some platforms. mt19937_64 is a 64-bit Mersenne Twister with a period of 2^19937 minus 1, and its output sequence is fully specified by the standard. The same seed gives the same integers on every conforming implementation.
Output:
first engine output: 13930160852258120406
normal 0: 1.301080
normal 1: 0.717408
normal 2: 0.158268
The distributions are different: the algorithm behind std::normal_distribution is implementation-defined. libstdc++ and libc++ produce different normals from the same engine state, so the same seed does not give the same risk numbers across compilers.
Interview trap: 'I set the seed, so the run is reproducible' holds only on one standard library. Pin the toolchain, or generate the uniforms and transform them yourself (next card).

Headline: take the engine's raw 64-bit output, which is specified exactly, and build the uniform yourself: \(u=((x\gg 11)+0.5)/2^{53}\in(0,1)\). Then apply Box-Muller: \(z=\sqrt{-2\ln u_1}\cos(2\pi u_2)\). Do not use uniform_real_distribution or normal_distribution, because both are implementation-defined.
Output:
z 0: -0.481218
z 1: 0.494584
z 2: 0.374554
What still breaks it: std::log and std::cos come from the system math library, which is not required to be correctly rounded, so the last bit can differ between libms. Compiler options such as -ffast-math and FMA contraction change rounding too.
Interview trap: the fix for a last-bit difference is a tolerance in the regression test, not a different seed. Document which math library produced the golden numbers.

Headline: std::string_view is a non-owning pointer and length. deskLabel returns a view of a local std::string, which is destroyed on return, so the view dangles. This is undefined behaviour.
The plain binary printed rates-gbp and then a garbage line (its contents vary). With -fsanitize=address and ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1, the sanitizer reports stack-use-after-return on the read in fwrite.
Fix: return std::string by value.
Interview trap: std::string_view sv = std::string("x") + y; dangles at the semicolon. A view of a string literal is safe because the literal has static storage. A string_view is not null-terminated, so it cannot be passed to C APIs through data() without a length.

Headline: a replacement field is {index:spec}, where the spec gives fill, alignment, width, zero padding, precision and type. The format string is checked at compile time, so a malformed spec is a compile error, not a runtime exception.
Output:
3.8567% |      12345 | 2y  | -0001.50
1.234500e+03
25 bp = 0.0025
{:>10} right-aligns to width 10, {:08.2f} pads with zeros to width 8, and {:e} gives scientific notation.
Interview trap: std::format does not insert thousands separators unless you use the locale-aware L form. For a DV01 report, format grouping explicitly.

Headline: a rehash invalidates all iterators, but it does not invalidate pointers or references to elements, because the nodes are not moved. The reference ref is still valid and prints 1.5. The iterator it must not be used after the inserts.
Output:
size 999
ref 1.5
This is the opposite of std::vector, where reallocation moves every element and invalidates references as well.
Interview trap: 'the reference survives' is a property of node-based containers, not of inserts in general. Erasing that element still invalidates the reference, and a vector gives no such guarantee on insert.
